question: TalkBack lands on the icon in your app bar and says only "button" — what is Flutter reporting, and what is the smallest fix?
answer:
An `Icon` is a glyph from a font with no text in it, so the semantics node gets a button role and a tap action but no name for the screen reader to read.

### The smallest fix
- `IconButton(tooltip: 'Search', ...)`. `IconButton` wraps itself in a `Tooltip` when you pass one, and `Tooltip` emits `Semantics(tooltip: message)`. On iOS the engine folds that into the accessibility label; on Android it becomes the node's tooltip text, which TalkBack reads. Sighted users get the long-press tooltip for free, which is why this is the recommended fix and not a workaround.

### The other two ways
- `Icon(Icons.search, semanticLabel: 'Search')` — for an icon that is not inside a button.
- `Semantics(button: true, label: 'Search', child: GestureDetector(...))` — a bare `GestureDetector` produces no role at all, so it needs both the flag and the label.

### Traps
- Label the action, not the picture: "More options", not "three dots" and not `more_vert`.
- Do not put "button" or "tap to" in the label. The role is already announced, and the platform already says the gesture; a hint belongs in `hint`.
- Decorative icons and spacer images should disappear, not be labelled: `ExcludeSemantics`, or `excludeFromSemantics: true` on `Image`. An unlabelled decorative node is one more swipe stop for no reason.

Rule of thumb: every tappable thing needs a name that reads as a verb phrase, and everything else needs to be invisible to the tree.

question: You wire up your first ARB file and `AppLocalizations.of(context)` comes back null at runtime — what is missing?
answer:
`AppLocalizations.of` is an `InheritedWidget` lookup, so it finds nothing unless the delegate is registered strictly above the context you handed it.

### What generates the class
- `flutter pub add flutter_localizations --sdk=flutter` plus `intl`.
- An `l10n.yaml` at the project root. Defaults: `arb-dir: lib/l10n`, `template-arb-file: app_en.arb`, `output-localization-file: app_localizations.dart`.
- `flutter gen-l10n`, which also runs automatically on `flutter run` and on every build once `l10n.yaml` exists. Output lands next to the ARB files — `lib/l10n/app_localizations.dart`, imported by a normal path. The old synthetic `package:flutter_gen` import is gone: `synthetic-package` is a deprecated flag that can no longer be turned on.
- Every key in `app_en.arb` becomes a getter or method; `app_ru.arb` supplies the same keys translated.

### What has to be above the context
- `MaterialApp(localizationsDelegates: AppLocalizations.localizationsDelegates, supportedLocales: AppLocalizations.supportedLocales)`. That list also pulls in the Material, Widgets and Cupertino delegates, which is what translates "Cancel" inside a date picker.
- The classic null is calling `AppLocalizations.of(context)` in the same `build` that *creates* `MaterialApp` — that context sits above the `Localizations` widget the app inserts. Read it in a child, or from `MaterialApp.builder`.
- The getter is nullable by default, hence `of(context)!`. Set `nullable-getter: false` in `l10n.yaml` if you would rather get a readable assertion than a null.

Rule of thumb: if the string is on screen, the delegate is above it.

question: A product card with a title, a price and a tap target is announced as three separate stops — how do you make a screen reader treat it as one button?
answer:
Give the card one semantics node of its own with a role and a hand-written label, and stop the children from contributing nodes underneath it.

### The three text slots, and what goes in each
- **label** — the name of the thing: "Espresso machine, 249 euros". Static.
- **value** — the part that changes: "in cart", "72 percent", "3 of 10". Announced after the label, and re-announced when it changes.
- **hint** — the consequence of acting: "Opens product details". Never write "double tap" here — the platform already says the gesture. To rename the action itself, use `onTapHint`.

### Flags that set the role
`button`, `link`, `header` (with `headingLevel` for a level), `textField`, `image`, `selected`, `checked`, `expanded`. These are what put the node into VoiceOver's rotor and TalkBack's headings menu, and what makes "double tap to activate" appear at all.

### Merge, exclude, or both
- `MergeSemantics` folds descendants into one node and concatenates their labels — perfect for "Battery" + "87%" where the concatenation reads well.
- When it does not read well, take control: `Semantics(container: true, button: true, label: ..., child: ExcludeSemantics(child: card))`. The wrapper supplies the node, `ExcludeSemantics` deletes the children's.
- `explicitChildNodes: true` for the opposite case: a labelled container whose children must stay individually reachable.

The trap: `MergeSemantics` merges **actions** too. Two tappable children inside it collapse into one node, and one of the two taps becomes unreachable by screen reader. One node per thing the user can act on.

question: A filter changes the result count but a screen reader stays silent — how do you announce a change that has no widget of its own?
answer:
Mark the widget whose text changed as a live region; the direct announcement API is a last resort, and Android now actively discourages it.

### liveRegion is the default answer
- `Semantics(liveRegion: true, child: Text('$n results'))`. Every time that node's label changes, the screen reader speaks it without moving focus — exactly what you want for counts, validation errors and status text.
- Flutter's `SnackBar` already does this for you: its content is wrapped in `Semantics(container: true, liveRegion: true, onDismiss: ...)`, so it is announced and gains a dismiss action. A hand-rolled toast pushed into an `Overlay` gets neither.
- The node has to stay in the tree. Swapping the whole widget out for a differently-keyed one is a new node, not a changed one, and may not announce.

### When there is genuinely nothing on screen
- `SemanticsService.announce(message, textDirection)` is **deprecated** since 3.35 because it cannot address a specific view. Use `SemanticsService.sendAnnouncement(View.of(context), message, textDirection)`.
- Guard it with `MediaQuery.supportsAnnounceOf(context)`. Android deprecated `announceForAccessibility` — TalkBack clears its speech queue for it — so that flag is false there and the call is dropped. iOS and web honour it.
- `assertiveness: Assertiveness.assertive` interrupts instead of queueing, and is only implemented on web.

Traps: a live region on a rapidly ticking counter makes the app unusable, and announcing text that is also on screen makes the user hear it twice — once now, once when they swipe to it.

Rule of thumb: change a label the user can find; announce only what has no home.

question: Tab and switch control jump around your form in an order that makes no sense, though it looks fine on screen — what decides that order?
answer:
Geometry decides it, not the order you wrote the widgets in: the default `ReadingOrderTraversalPolicy` sorts focusable nodes by position under the current `Directionality`, so any layout that is not a clean reading order traverses badly.

### Two orders, two mechanisms
- **Keyboard, Tab, switch control** — the focus tree. `WidgetsApp` wraps the app in `FocusTraversalGroup(policy: ReadingOrderTraversalPolicy())`.
- **Screen reader swipe** — the semantics tree, reordered with `Semantics(sortKey: OrdinalSortKey(1))`.

They are separate. Setting a focus order changes nothing for TalkBack, and a sort key changes nothing for Tab. That is the trap that costs an afternoon.

### Fixing keyboard order
1. Group first. `FocusTraversalGroup` around a subtree makes traversal finish everything inside before moving on — one per column of a two-column layout, one per toolbar, one per dialog.
2. Order only when grouping cannot express it: `FocusTraversalGroup(policy: OrderedTraversalPolicy())` plus `FocusTraversalOrder(order: NumericFocusOrder(2), child: ...)`. `LexicalFocusOrder` takes strings.
3. `WidgetOrderTraversalPolicy` follows the widget tree instead of the geometry — the escape hatch when the geometry is genuinely meaningless.
4. Remove what should not be a stop: `ExcludeFocus`, or `Focus(skipTraversal: true)` for a node that can hold focus programmatically but should not be tabbed to.

### Where it goes wrong most
A `Stack` or a `Wrap` has no reading order to infer, so overlapping or reflowed children get sorted by raw offsets. Dialogs are the other one: autofocus into the dialog when it opens and restore the previous focus when it closes, or focus falls back to the top of the page.

question: An audit flags your custom chip row for tap target size and contrast but passes the Material buttons beside it — what is Material doing that your widget is not?
answer:
Material pads a control's hit area out to 48x48 independently of how big it looks, and takes its colours from a `ColorScheme` whose pairs are contrast-checked; a `GestureDetector` around a 24 dp icon gets exactly 24 dp and whatever colour you typed.

### Tap targets
- `kMinInteractiveDimension` is 48.0, and `ThemeData.materialTapTargetSize` defaults to `MaterialTapTargetSize.padded`, which expands `IconButton`, `Checkbox`, `Radio`, `Switch` and the button family to that box. `IconButton`'s default constraints are `minWidth`/`minHeight: kMinInteractiveDimension`.
- The guidelines are 48x48 dp on Android and 44x44 pt on iOS, with roughly 8 dp between neighbouring targets.
- For a custom widget, size the *hit area*, not the glyph: put a `SizedBox` or `ConstrainedBox` around the `InkWell`, and keep the padding **inside** the gesture detector. Padding applied outside it is not part of the hit test and buys nothing.
- `visualDensity: VisualDensity.compact` and `materialTapTargetSize: shrinkWrap` pull Material's own controls back below the guideline. If someone set either app-wide to tighten a dense screen, that is usually the line the audit found.

### Contrast
- WCAG wants 4.5:1 for body text, and 3:1 for large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold) and for the boundaries of icons and controls.
- `ColorScheme` exists so `onPrimary` on `primary` clears the bar. A hand-picked `Colors.grey.shade400` on white is about 2:1 and fails outright.
- The usual offenders: disabled states, hint and placeholder text, and any text drawn over a photo without a scrim.

Rule of thumb: the target is the hit-test rectangle and the colour is a pair, never a single value.

question: A user turns on Reduce Motion and your onboarding still slides and parallaxes — which MediaQuery flags exist, and what should the UI actually change?
answer:
Flutter surfaces the platform's accessibility switches on `MediaQueryData`, but nothing reads them for you — the single exception is `Text`, which merges in `FontWeight.bold` on its own when bold text is requested.

### The flags, and where they are real
- `MediaQuery.disableAnimationsOf(context)` — iOS Reduce Motion and an Android animator duration scale of 0. The only motion flag that works on both platforms.
- `MediaQuery.boldTextOf(context)` — iOS and Android API 31+. `Text` already applies it, so your job is a layout that survives wider glyphs.
- `MediaQuery.highContrastOf(context)`, `invertColorsOf`, `onOffSwitchLabelsOf` — **iOS only**; on Android they are permanently false, so never gate a feature on them alone.
- `MediaQuery.accessibleNavigationOf(context)` — true while TalkBack or VoiceOver is running.
- `MediaQuery.textScalerOf(context)` returns a `TextScaler`; the old `textScaleFactor` double is deprecated because scaling is now non-linear. It goes past 2x on both platforms.

### What to actually change
- Replace movement with a cross-fade or a cut. Keep the state change, drop the travel — shortening the duration is not the same thing.
- Stop auto-advancing carousels, parallax headers and looping hero animations entirely.
- Under `accessibleNavigation`, drop hover-only affordances and anything that dismisses itself on a timer.
- `highContrast` needs no code: pass `highContrastTheme` and `highContrastDarkTheme` to `MaterialApp` and it swaps them in itself.

Rule of thumb: reduce motion means no vestibular motion, not no feedback — the user still needs to know something happened.

question: The Russian build renders "5 товар" instead of "5 товаров" — what is wrong with that message, and how do you write it so a translator can fix it?
answer:
The sentence was assembled in Dart by gluing a number onto a noun, so no translator ever saw the whole message and there was nowhere to express Russian's plural rules; plural selection belongs inside the ARB message as ICU.

### Placeholders
Every placeholder is declared in the `@key` metadata, and the type decides the generated signature.

- `"greeting": "Hello, {name}!"` with `"@greeting": {"description": "...", "placeholders": {"name": {"type": "String"}}}` generates `l10n.greeting(name)`.
- `description` is the only context the translator gets. Write it.

### plural
- `"cartItems": "{count, plural, =0{Cart is empty} one{{count} item} other{{count} items}}"`, with `"count": {"type": "num"}`.
- The categories are `zero one two few many other`, plus exact matches `=0`, `=1`, `=2`. Which ones a language needs is a property of that language, not of your message: English uses `one`/`other`, Russian needs `one`, `few` and `many` — 1 товар, 2 товара, 5 товаров. `app_ru.arb` adds the cases it needs; the English template does not have to list them.

### select
`"invitedBy": "{gender, select, male{He invited you} female{She invited you} other{They invited you}}"` — the same machinery for gender, plan tier, anything enumerable.

### The trap
Anything you concatenate outside ARB is untranslatable. `'Deleted ' + n.toString() + ' files'` cannot be pluralised or reordered, and splitting a sentence into two keys so you can bold the middle bakes English word order into the layout. One message per sentence — if part of it must be styled, pass the whole message through and mark it up in the widget.

question: A German user sees a price as $1,234.50 and a date as 12/03/2026, and a scheduled event shows the wrong hour — what did the formatting code get wrong?
answer:
Both bugs come from the same shortcut: formatting without a locale, and treating the device's timezone as the user's.

### Format through a skeleton, with an explicit locale
- `DateFormat.yMMMd(locale)` is a skeleton — it asks for "year, abbreviated month, day" and lets the locale decide the order and the separators. A literal pattern, `DateFormat('dd/MM/yyyy')`, freezes one country's convention forever.
- `NumberFormat.decimalPattern(locale)`, `NumberFormat.currency(locale: ..., symbol: ...)` and `NumberFormat.compact(locale: ...)` carry the grouping character, the decimal separator and which side the symbol sits on. German wants `1.234,50 €`, not `$1,234.50`.
- Pass the *app's* locale — `Localizations.localeOf(context).toString()` — not the device's. The two diverge the moment you ship an in-app language switch. With no locale at all, `intl` falls back to `Intl.defaultLocale`, which is `en_US` until you set it.
- `GlobalMaterialLocalizations` initialises date symbols for the locales it loads, so inside a `MaterialApp` you usually get them free. Outside one — a background isolate, a PDF export, a plain unit test — call `initializeDateFormatting(locale)` first or `DateFormat` throws `LocaleDataException`.

### Timezones
- A server sending `2026-03-12T18:00:00Z` parses into a UTC `DateTime`. Formatting it prints 18:00 UTC; `toLocal()` prints it in whatever zone the *phone* is in.
- That is correct for "when did this happen" and wrong for anything anchored to a place: a store's opening hours, a departure, a class. Those need the event's IANA zone through `package:timezone` and `tz.TZDateTime.from(...)`.
- `DateTime` carries no zone beyond a UTC flag, so you cannot store one in it — send the zone name as its own field.

Rule of thumb: store UTC, transport ISO-8601, and format at the very edge with a locale and a zone you chose on purpose.

question: The app comes up in English on a Spanish phone even though es.arb exists — how does Flutter pick a locale, and where does an in-app language switch hook in?
answer:
Flutter matches the user's ordered list of preferred locales against `supportedLocales`, and an app that is stubbornly English almost always never got `supportedLocales` and `localizationsDelegates` at all — `WidgetsApp` then defaults to `[Locale('en', 'US')]`.

### The resolution order
1. `MaterialApp.locale`, when non-null, wins outright and the system list is ignored. That is the hook for an in-app switch.
2. `localeListResolutionCallback(preferred, supported)` if you supplied one — it sees the whole ordered list the OS reports, which is the only way to honour a second preference.
3. `localeResolutionCallback`, the older single-locale variant; prefer the list version.
4. Otherwise `basicLocaleListResolution`: for each preferred locale in turn, an exact language+script+country match, then language+script, then language+country, then language alone. Nothing matches at all → `supportedLocales.first`, which is why the order of that list matters.

Returning `null` from either callback falls through to the default algorithm — return a real `Locale` only when you mean to override it.

### The in-app switch
- Hold a `Locale?` wherever app-wide state lives, with `null` meaning "follow the system", and feed it to `MaterialApp.locale`. Rebuilding the `MaterialApp` re-runs `Localizations`, and every `AppLocalizations.of(context)` below it picks up the new strings.
- Persist the choice and read it back *before* `runApp`, or the first frame flashes the system language.
- Use the generated `AppLocalizations.supportedLocales` and `.localizationsDelegates` rather than a hand-written list: a locale you list but never translated makes the delegate throw on load.
- Set `Intl.defaultLocale` alongside it if anything formats dates or numbers outside the widget tree.

Mental model: the system locale is a default, not the truth. `supportedLocales` is a contract, and its first entry is your fallback language.

question: In Arabic your row's icon stays on the left and the padding sits on the wrong side — what mirrors automatically in Flutter and what never will?
answer:
Everything that reads the ambient `Directionality` mirrors itself, and everything that names a physical side does not — so `Row` and `EdgeInsetsDirectional` flip while `EdgeInsets.only(left:)` and `Positioned(left:)` stay exactly where you put them.

### Where the direction comes from
- `MaterialApp` installs a `Directionality` above your app from the resolved locale, via `GlobalWidgetsLocalizations` — ar, he, fa and ur report `TextDirection.rtl`. Read it with `Directionality.of(context)`, or wrap a subtree to force one.
- `Row`, `MainAxisAlignment.start`/`.end`, a horizontal `ListView` and `TextAlign.start` are already directional: they mean "leading", not "left".

### Swap these, one for one
- `EdgeInsets.only(left:, right:)` → `EdgeInsetsDirectional.only(start:, end:)`
- `Alignment.centerLeft` → `AlignmentDirectional.centerStart`
- `Positioned(left:)` → `PositionedDirectional(start:)`
- `BorderRadius.only(topLeft:)` → `BorderRadiusDirectional.only(topStart:)`
- `TextAlign.left` → `TextAlign.start`

### Icons
Material's directional glyphs — `Icons.arrow_back`, `Icons.chevron_left`, `Icons.arrow_forward_ios` — are declared with `matchTextDirection: true`, and the `Icon` widget flips them for you. A custom SVG or PNG has no such flag, so mirror it yourself with `Transform.flip`. Some icons must never mirror: media transport controls, a clock, a checkmark, your logo, anything showing a number.

The trap that survives code review is the leftover physical offset: the layout mirrors correctly but a hardcoded `Offset(8, 0)`, an `Alignment(-1, 0)` or a `Transform.translate` does not, so the badge lands off the avatar and only in Arabic. Preview it by wrapping the whole app in a forced `Directionality.rtl` from day one, rather than waiting for the Arabic build.

question: Your widget tests assert on find.text('Save') and a German screen still shipped untranslated — how should localized UI actually be tested?
answer:
Pump the widget inside a real `Localizations` scope and assert against the same generated getter the UI calls, so the test proves the wiring instead of pinning one language's copy.

### Pumping under a locale
- Give the test's `MaterialApp` the generated `localizationsDelegates` and `supportedLocales` plus an explicit `locale:`. Without the delegates, `AppLocalizations.of(context)!` throws a null check error and the failure looks like a widget bug.
- To exercise resolution itself rather than a fixed locale, set `tester.platformDispatcher.localesTestValue` and register `clearLocalesTestValue` in `addTearDown` — leaking it poisons every later test in the file.
- The generated delegate loads synchronously, so a single `pump()` is enough; you do not need `pumpAndSettle` just to get strings.

### Assert on the key, not the sentence
- Load the strings the same way the app does: `await AppLocalizations.delegate.load(const Locale('de'))`, then `expect(find.text(l10n.saveButton), findsOneWidget)`. The test now fails when the key disappears or the widget stops being localized, and survives a copywriter changing the English.
- When the visible text is not the point, `find.byKey` and `find.bySemanticsLabel` say what you mean more directly.
- Test the locale-sensitive *behaviour* once each — a plural crossing from one to five, a date skeleton, an RTL layout — rather than repeating one test twenty times.

### What a widget test cannot catch
A missing translation is a build problem, not a test one: set `untranslated-messages-file` in `l10n.yaml` and fail the release job when that report is not empty. Overflow at German length is a golden test on your two or three densest screens, not on all of them.

question: The backend returns {"code": "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS"} and your Bloc stores the sentence it will show — what breaks, and where does translation belong?
answer:
Translation belongs at the presentation edge: the data layer turns the wire code into a typed failure, the widget turns that failure into a string with `AppLocalizations`, and nothing in between ever holds display text.

### Why a translated string in state is a bug
- Switch the language and the state object still holds the old sentence. Nothing recomputes it, so the screen changes and the error message does not — the classic report from a QA engineer who toggles languages.
- Producing the string needs a `BuildContext`, which drags `context` into a repository or a Bloc that must not have one.
- The state can then only be asserted against English prose, so a copy edit breaks a business-logic test.

### The shape that works
1. The server sends a stable machine code plus structured params: `{"code": "INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS", "params": {"shortfall": "12.40"}}`. Server prose is unversioned, untranslatable and impossible to fit into your layout.
2. The data layer maps the code onto your existing typed failure — the params travel as data, never as a formatted sentence.
3. The widget switches over the failure and calls the matching ARB message with those params. There is deliberately no `l10n['someKey']` lookup: gen-l10n emits one getter per message, so a server-invented key cannot silently render blank.
4. An unknown code falls back to a generic message that still prints the raw code, so support can act on a screenshot.

### Content the server genuinely owns
Catalogue names, CMS copy and promo banners cannot live in ARB. Send `Accept-Language` built from the *app's* locale rather than `Platform.localeName`, let the server walk its own fallback chain, and key every disk cache by locale — otherwise a language switch serves yesterday's language from a database that has no idea a locale exists.

Rule of thumb: codes cross the network, sentences never do.

question: A PR adds an icon-only toolbar — what can a widget test actually prove about its accessibility, and what still needs a device with TalkBack on?
answer:
Widget tests can prove the mechanical rules — tap-target size, contrast, that every tappable node carries a label — through `meetsGuideline`, but nothing automated can tell you whether what the screen reader says makes sense in the order it says it.

### In a widget test
- Call `tester.ensureSemantics()` first and dispose the handle afterwards. Flutter does not build a semantics tree unless a client has asked for one, so without that handle `meetsGuideline` and `tester.getSemantics` have nothing to look at and the assertions are vacuous.
- The four shipped guidelines are `androidTapTargetGuideline` (48dp), `iOSTapTargetGuideline` (44pt), `labeledTapTargetGuideline` and `textContrastGuideline` (WCAG AA, 4.5:1). Run them with `await expectLater(tester, meetsGuideline(...))`.
- For one specific node, `matchesSemantics` and the looser `containsSemantics` assert the label, the flags and the available actions on the result of `tester.getSemantics(finder)`.

### On the machine in front of you
- `SemanticsDebugger` wrapped around the app draws every node with its label; `debugDumpSemanticsTree()` prints the same structure to the console.
- Because the tree is exported to the platform, Android's Accessibility Scanner and Xcode's Accessibility Inspector both audit a running Flutter app for real.

### What only a human pass finds
Traversal order that is legal but nonsensical, a label that reads out as "archive button button", a live region that interrupts on every keystroke, a custom swipe that TalkBack has already claimed, and a dialog that never moves focus into itself. `textContrastGuideline` also decides foreground and background from the rendered pixels, so its verdict on text over a photo or a gradient is the one you should trust least — and that is exactly where contrast fails.

Rule: automate the numbers, then walk the screen with the reader switched on before you call it done.

question: TalkBack reads your revenue chart as one empty box — how do you give a CustomPainter or a custom RenderObject real semantics?
answer:
A `CustomPaint` contributes nothing to the semantics tree unless you supply `semanticsBuilder`, because a canvas produces pixels and the accessibility bridge only ships nodes.

### Two options for CustomPaint
1. **One summary node.** Wrap the chart in `Semantics(label: ...)` with a sentence a person would actually want read — "Revenue, twelve months, 3.2 thousand in January rising to 9.8 thousand in December" — and `ExcludeSemantics` anything decorative inside. For most charts this is more useful than twelve focus stops.
2. **`semanticsBuilder`** on the painter, returning one `CustomPainterSemantics` per region, each with a `rect` and a `SemanticsProperties`. Override `shouldRebuildSemantics(oldDelegate)` as well — it is a separate callback from `shouldRepaint`, and returning `false` there freezes the labels while the pixels keep updating, which is the bug you will spend an afternoon on.

Rects are in the painter's own coordinate space and must be non-empty; a zero-size or completely covered rect yields a node the reader can never focus. A `label` also requires a `textDirection` — `SemanticsData` asserts on a labelled node without one.

### A custom RenderObject
Override `describeSemanticsConfiguration(SemanticsConfiguration config)`: set `config.isSemanticBoundary`, `label`, `value`, `textDirection`, and actions such as `onTap`, or `onIncrease`/`onDecrease` for anything slider-shaped, so the rotor and TalkBack's volume gestures work. Then call `markNeedsSemanticsUpdate()` whenever the underlying data changes — `markNeedsPaint()` does not imply it. When one render object should expose several nodes, override `assembleSemanticsNode`.

Trap worth naming: text you laid out with a `TextPainter` and drew on the canvas is invisible for exactly the same reason, so an axis label is not a label.

Rule: if you painted it, you also have to say it.

question: You are adding nineteen languages to an app that has one — what goes into CI, and what will break first in German and Japanese?
answer:
Make one English ARB the single source of truth, move it to and from a translation system through CI, gate the build on completeness — and find the layout damage with pseudo-localization long before a translator sees the app.

### The pipeline
- One source file, `app_en.arb`, with an `@key` description and placeholder metadata on every message. That description is the entire context a translator gets, and a key reused for a noun and a verb will come back wrong in half the languages.
- CI pushes the source on merge and opens a pull request with the returned ARBs. Translated files are generated artefacts — nobody hand-edits them in the repo.
- Set `untranslated-messages-file` in `l10n.yaml` and fail the release job when the report lists anything for a shipping locale. Malformed ICU fails `flutter gen-l10n` outright, so it breaks the PR rather than the store listing.

### Pseudo-localization
Generate a fake locale from the source ARB — accented glyphs, brackets around each message, roughly 40% padding — and register it in debug builds only. One pass finds three classes of bug at once: hardcoded strings stay plain ASCII, tight layouts overflow, and messages assembled from fragments show their seams. Android's `en-XA` system pseudolocale does not help here, because your ARBs contain no such locale.

### What breaks
- German and Russian run roughly a third longer than English, so fixed-width buttons, single-line `Row`s and `maxLines: 1` chips overflow. `Flexible` plus wrapping is the fix; `FittedBox` is the last resort, because shrinking text below the platform minimum is its own accessibility failure.
- Japanese and Chinese are shorter but break lines almost anywhere, so a two-word label splits in the middle of a term; Arabic and Devanagari need more line height than your hardcoded `height:` allows.
- Golden tests per locale on the two densest screens, not on all twenty.
